title: Though the fig tree (Habakkuk 3:17–19)
hookLine: no fruit, no flock, and yet I will rejoice

cards: A prophet's usual job is to speak to the people for God. Habakkuk talks back to God. His book opens with a complaint, in the King James Bible: "O LORD, how long shall I cry, and thou wilt not hear!"
Violence everywhere, the law ignored, the wicked winning. God's answer makes it worse: the Babylonians are coming, a fierce army that will sweep through like the desert wind.
So Habakkuk climbs a watchtower, in his words, to wait and see what God will say. Three short chapters later, he comes down singing.

teach.b: The song ends with Habakkuk imagining the worst.

In the King James: "Although the fig tree shall not blossom, neither shall fruit be in the vines; the labour of the olive shall fail, and the fields shall yield no meat; the flock shall be cut off from the fold, and there shall be no herd in the stalls."
Count it. Figs, grapes, olives, grain, sheep, cattle. For a farming people, that's everything: the pantry, the bank account, the retirement plan.
Then one small word: "Yet I will rejoice in the LORD, I will joy in the God of my salvation." Yet. Habakkuk doesn't say things will turn out fine, or that the fig tree will bloom after all.

teach.h: NOT IF IT BLOOMS. EVEN IF IT DOESN'T.
teach.b: He says: even if it doesn't. His joy is anchored somewhere the harvest can't reach.

teach.h: FEET LIKE A DEER'S ON THE ROCKS.
teach.b: Then the last picture: "he will make my feet like hinds' feet." A hind is a female deer, and in those hills deer pick their way up steep, rocky slopes without falling. The ground doesn't get easier.

teach.h: YET I WILL REJOICE IN THE LORD.
teach.b: The book ends with a note for the choir leader about stringed instruments: this cry of faith from the edge of disaster was meant to be sung together.

Some Christians turn to these verses in hard seasons, and some read Habakkuk as a pattern for honest prayer: complain first, wait on the watchtower, then sing. The yet doesn't cancel the complaint. It comes after it.

how: Some Christians turn to Habakkuk 3:17–18 in times of loss, and its words have been set in hymns and songs; Habakkuk 2:4, on the just living by faith, is quoted in Romans, Galatians and Hebrews.

o: deer's feet, sure on steep and rocky ground
feet sore and tired from a long journey
the bare feet of a servant in the house

games.q: what's inside Habakkuk — tap the pairs.
p: where he waits for God's answer
a deer's sure step on rocky hills
a note for the choir leader

s: Habakkuk says the fig tree will bloom again
he never promises that. he says even if it doesn't, yet I will rejoice.
Habakkuk complains to God out loud
his book opens with "O LORD, how long shall I cry, and thou wilt not hear!"
the song was meant to be sung
it ends with a note for the chief singer, on stringed instruments.

games.q: you're a farmer. the figs didn't blossom, the olives failed, the sheep are gone. what does Habakkuk do?
o: name it all, and rejoice anyway.
games.why: he lists every loss honestly, and then says "yet I will rejoice in the LORD." the yet comes after the complaint, not instead of it.

practice: If today is hard, let it be hard, and name what's not blooming, money, health, a relationship, plans that fell apart, plainly, the way Habakkuk listed his empty fields.
Then look for one thing that's still good, a person who loves you, light through a window, a song you know by heart, and rest your attention there.
If you pray, say Habakkuk's yet in your own heart; if not, let that one good thing be enough for now.

wordCard.voice: Hinds' feet. What Habakkuk says God gives him for climbing steep, rocky ground: not an easier path, but surer footing.

orig.note: Hebrew: but I, yet I. the first word of Habakkuk 3:18, the turn of the whole song.

carryVoice: Your line: yet I will rejoice. The ground stays steep; the feet get surer. That's day four hundred ninety-one.
